title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
coreMove: Expose comfortable adequacy as a decision to stop investigating what greatness would require.
sourcePressure: The source frames good results as the trap that prevents a leap and grounds the argument in comparative research: 11 good-to-great companies, matched comparisons, and sustained results over a long horizon.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says greatness comes from a dramatic breakthrough, a charismatic push, or wanting excellence harder.
sourceAlignmentTerms: good is the enemy of great

hook: a generic company offsite deciding to be great
tryThisNow: rate your life from one to ten
write down where you want excellence

exampleSpecs.audience: a radiology director whose department meets the published wait-time benchmark
exampleSpecs.stakes: patients with suspicious scans are still waiting long enough for surgeons to lose treatment options
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director places the benchmark report beside a handwritten list of delayed cancer follow-ups and circles the gap between acceptable and great care
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stack of MRI request forms under the green glow of the scanner console

exampleSpecs.audience: a store owner proud of steady monthly revenue
exampleSpecs.stakes: steady sales hide the loss of browsing traffic that used to create loyal customers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner pins last year's receipt roll beside this year's door-counter tape and sees that the same dollars now come from fewer, less curious buyers
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a receipt roll curling over the edge of a crowded checkout drawer

exampleSpecs.audience: an operations manager whose food stands score well on postgame surveys
exampleSpecs.stakes: fans abandon long lines during the third inning and never show up in satisfaction averages
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager stands behind the pretzel warmer and marks every fan who leaves the line before ordering, then compares that count with the cheerful survey score
exampleSpecs.firstImage: steam fogging the glass of a pretzel warmer while the home team comes to bat

exampleSpecs.audience: a library director whose e-card launch met its signup target
exampleSpecs.stakes: rural patrons remain absent even though the rollout is being celebrated as successful
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director lays a zip-code heat map over the signup target sheet and sees the empty towns the target allowed everyone to ignore
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a laminated county map spread across the reference desk before opening

exampleSpecs.audience: an outfitter owner proud of a season with no reportable injuries
exampleSpecs.stakes: near misses on one rapid show that no-injury status is hiding a fragile operation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner asks guides to sort wet incident cards by rapid and watches one rock garden form a pile that the official injury log never showed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: damp incident cards drying on a paddleboard rack

exampleSpecs.audience: a gate supervisor whose flights depart within the airline's accepted window
exampleSpecs.stakes: families with tight connections still miss flights while the station reports on-time success
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor replays the scanner timestamps for one family and watches the acceptable departure metric erase their missed connection
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a boarding scanner blinking amber beside a stroller tag
mustAvoid: technology failure as the main point

skillTargets: spot metrics that certify good while hiding greatness gaps
distinguish cumulative evidence from breakthrough mythology
choose comparison groups that reveal complacency
identify when adequate performance has become a ceiling

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one result you call good. Put its official metric beside one ignored consequence from the same work, then write the question that comparison forces you to ask.

sourceAnchors.name: Collins comparative study
sourceAnchors.detail: the source says Collins and his team identified organizations that made a durable leap and compared them with similar firms that did not
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The claim has weight because the leap is held against companies close enough to make comfort look costly.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
